notes.label: Congestion window
notes.summary: A TCP sender uses a congestion window to bound outstanding network data, separate from the receiving endpoint's advertised window.
boundaries: This describes sender congestion control, not every queuing policy.

notes.label: Slow start and congestion avoidance
notes.summary: TCP begins by probing network capacity and changes growth behaviour according to the slow-start threshold and congestion signals.
assumptions: Acknowledgments and congestion signals are observed
boundaries: TCP's congestion state is not a direct measurement of warehouse demand.

notes.label: Congestion response to packet loss
notes.summary: Loss-based TCP congestion control responds to indications of congestion rather than assuming network capacity remains constant.
assumptions: Packet loss is used as a congestion signal
boundaries: A packet can be lost for reasons other than congestion.

notes.label: Explicit congestion notification
notes.summary: ECN allows compliant network endpoints to react to explicit congestion marks rather than relying exclusively on dropped packets.
boundaries: Congestion marking is not a general-purpose biological sensor.

notes.label: Sensors and regulated variables
notes.summary: A homeostatic control mechanism requires measurement of a regulated physiological variable and an appropriate corrective response.
boundaries: Negative feedback alone does not make a system homeostatic.

notes.label: Controller and effector
notes.summary: Sensors communicate deviations to control mechanisms, while effectors change bodily processes that influence the regulated variable.
assumptions: Sensor and effector pathways are active
boundaries: The simplified diagram omits many physiological interactions.

notes.label: Feedforward versus negative feedback
notes.summary: Biological regulation may use anticipatory feedforward actions and buffering in addition to reactive feedback after disturbances.
assumptions: The organism can anticipate certain disturbances
boundaries: Anticipation is not a guarantee of perfect predictions.

notes.label: Limits of simplistic feedback analogy
notes.summary: Regulation combines several types of responses; a single simplified negative-feedback loop is insufficient for every organism-level process.
boundaries: No universal one-controller model follows from this note.

notes.label: Reorder point
notes.summary: Reorder-point planning compares projected inventory against expected usage during replenishment lead time plus safety stock.
assumptions: Lead time and demand estimates available
boundaries: Different inventory platforms implement different planning conventions.

notes.label: Lead time and reorder timing
notes.summary: Planners use the reorder threshold to initiate supply early enough to cover demand until replenishment arrives.
boundaries: Unexpected supplier delay can invalidate expected coverage.

notes.label: Safety stock
notes.summary: A safety inventory buffer helps reduce stockout risk during demand spikes or delays in obtaining additional supplies.
boundaries: Excess buffers impose costs and do not eliminate stockout risk.
notes.source_anchor: Safety stock fulfillment for items / How master planning handles the constraint

notes.label: Inventory priority tradeoff
notes.summary: Certain master-planning decisions prioritise meeting actual orders over restoring a nominal safety buffer to avoid delaying fulfilment.
assumptions: System planning setting permits such priorities
boundaries: Implementation can vary with settings and planning engine.
